objectives: Reason about BMI signal acquisition + decoding.

slides.title: Prosthetic limbs: from passive to neural
slides.body:
**Prosthetic upper + lower limbs** ranges:
• **Passive**: cosmetic; no movement. Lightweight.
• **Body-powered**: cables actuated by shoulder or hip movement. Reliable, durable, no batteries. Limited dexterity. Standard for many amputees globally.
• **Myoelectric**: EMG (electromyography) signals from residual muscle drive motors. Multi-finger control. Battery-powered. Commercial: Ottobock Michelangelo, Touch Bionics i-Limb, BeBionic.
• **Powered**: motor + battery for joint motion (knee, ankle). Examples: Ottobock C-Leg + Genium (knee with microprocessor); Össur Power Knee.
• **Sensory feedback**: vibrotactile + intraneural stimulation in research (LifeHand 2, DARPA HAPTIX). Restores touch + position sense; reduces phantom-limb pain.
• **Bone-anchored** (osseointegration): titanium implant through skin to bone (skull, femur, humerus). Improved attachment, reduced soft-tissue issues. ~5000+ implants since 1990.
• **Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)**: surgically reroute amputated nerves to alternative muscles; provides additional EMG control signals + reduces neuroma + phantom pain.

**Lower-limb microprocessor knees** (C-Leg, X3, RHEO, Genium): sensors track gait phase + adjust hydraulic damping in real time → near-natural walking on stairs + slopes + variable terrain. Improved fall prevention vs passive knees.

**Foot prostheses**: Össur Cheetah blade (carbon-fiber spring) for running; Power Foot (Ottobock Empower) with powered ankle for level walking + slopes.

slides.title: Brain-machine interfaces: signal acquisition
slides.body:
**Brain-machine interfaces (BMI / BCI)** record neural activity + decode intent to control devices. Spectrum of invasiveness:

**Non-invasive**:
• **EEG (electroencephalography)**: scalp electrodes; ~100 ms temporal resolution; ~cm spatial. P300 spellers, SSVEP-based; portable; established assistive technology (BrainGate-Communicate). Low bandwidth (~bits/min for typing).
• **fNIRS** (functional near-IR spectroscopy): hemodynamic; slower; portable; research.
• **MEG** (magnetoencephalography): superconducting sensors; sub-mm spatial; hospital-only; large.

**Minimally invasive**:
• **Stentrode** (Synchron): self-expanding stent with electrodes deployed in cerebral venous sinus; no craniotomy. Approved for ALS trials; ~10 patients implanted by 2024.
• **Sub-scalp** electrodes: clinical for epilepsy monitoring.

**Invasive**:
• **ECoG / subdural grids**: electrodes on cortical surface (under dura). Used clinically for epilepsy mapping + experimental BMI.
• **Utah array**: silicon-based 96-electrode array, ~1 mm × 4 mm; penetrates cortex 1.5 mm. Records single-unit + LFP. BrainGate (academic consortium) + clinical trials.
• **Microwire arrays**: emerging.
• **Neuralink**: thin polymer threads (~5 μm) with 1024+ electrodes per chip; robotic-implanted; bi-directional. First human implant Jan 2024 (Noland Arbaugh).
• **Paradromics**: high-bandwidth electrode arrays.

**Trade-off**: invasiveness vs signal quality vs longevity. Utah arrays degrade over months-years (foreign-body response encapsulates electrodes); Neuralink + others aim to extend with biocompatible materials + soft electrodes.

slides.title: Neural decoding + clinical applications
slides.body:
**Decoding pipeline**:
1. **Signal preprocessing**: filter, denoise, spike detection (threshold or template matching).
2. **Feature extraction**: firing rates, LFP power spectra, spike sorting (single units).
3. **Decoder**: linear (Kalman filter, Wiener filter); nonlinear (RNN, deep learning).
4. **Effector control**: cursor, robotic arm, speech synthesis, mouse.
5. **Feedback loop**: visual + (sometimes) sensory feedback for adaptation.

**Major demonstrations** (clinical + research):
- **BrainGate** (Cleveland Clinic + collaborators): tetraplegic patients control cursor, robotic arm. Cathy Hutchinson (2012) self-fed via prosthetic arm.
- **Speech BCI**: Edward Chang's group (UCSF, 2021-23): cortical recordings decoded to speech text + articulation. Real-time speech-via-BCI ~40-80 wpm.
- **Visual BCI**: Argus II retinal implant (Second Sight, 2013 FDA approval; company bankruptcy 2022); cortical implants in trials.
- **Hearing**: cochlear implant pioneer (analog signal processing into auditory nerve); ~1M users globally.
- **Synchron**: minimally invasive BMI for ALS patients (Stentrode); FDA breakthrough designation.
- **Neuralink**: first human implant (2024); cursor control demonstrated. Long-term performance + safety + scaling unknown.

**Clinical applications**:
- **ALS / locked-in syndrome**: communication + basic control.
- **Tetraplegia**: limb control via robotic arm + functional electrical stimulation.
- **Parkinson's + tremor + dystonia**: deep brain stimulation (DBS, Medtronic + Boston Scientific + Abbott) — established therapy since 1997; ~200K implants globally.
- **Epilepsy**: responsive neurostimulation (RNS, NeuroPace), DBS, vagus nerve stimulation.
- **Depression + OCD** (treatment-resistant): DBS + emerging closed-loop personalized; mixed clinical results so far.
- **Spinal cord injury**: epidural stimulation + brain-spine interfaces (Courtine + collaborators) restoring walking in paraplegic patients.

**Ethics + open questions**:
- Informed consent for novel + experimental devices.
- Privacy of neural data (BNeuro / BCI privacy laws in Chile + Colorado).
- Cognitive enhancement vs treatment.
- Long-term safety + revision.
- Equity + access (BMI cost ~$100K-$1M).

question.question: Design a basic EEG-based BCI cursor control system
question.goal: Design a non-invasive BCI for cursor control via EEG.

steps.prompt: What EEG paradigm gives a usable signal?
steps.reveal:
Three main paradigms:
- **P300**: event-related potential ~300 ms after target stimulus (oddball). Used in spellers.
- **SSVEP** (steady-state visual evoked potential): EEG matches frequency of flickering target. Multiple flicker frequencies → discrete choices.
- **Motor imagery**: imagining left vs right hand movement → mu/beta rhythm modulation over sensorimotor cortex.
For cursor control: motor imagery → 2D control; or SSVEP for discrete direction choices.

Pipeline:
1. Bandpass filter 8-30 Hz (mu + beta band).
2. Artifact rejection (eye blinks, muscle).
3. Feature extraction: Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) — supervised filter that maximizes variance ratio between classes.
4. Classifier: LDA, SVM, or shallow CNN.
5. Smoothing / Kalman filter for cursor trajectory.
6. Adaptation: continuous model update as user learns.

Limitations: low bit rate (~25-50 bits/min vs invasive 50+ bits/sec); requires user training (weeks-months); session-to-session variability; sensitive to electrode placement + impedance + artifacts; limited to ~4-direction discrete control or 2D continuous with poor smoothness. EEG cursor BCIs deployed clinically for ALS communication but slow; advances in deep learning + transfer learning reducing training burden.

steps.prompt: When would invasive (Utah array, ECoG) be preferred?
steps.reveal: Invasive BMIs preferred when: (1) high-bandwidth output needed (>100 wpm speech, multi-DOF robotic arm); (2) tetraplegia with no alternative; (3) ALS late-stage with no other communication; (4) research clinical trial with full informed consent. Risk: craniotomy, infection, hemorrhage, ~10% revision rate over years. Benefit: 10-100× more information than EEG. Future: Neuralink + Synchron + others reducing surgical burden; ECoG semi-invasive with high signal quality. The 'minimally invasive' middle ground (Stentrode, sub-scalp) is the active frontier.

question.question: Drag the slider to estimate the typical number of electrodes on a Utah array (single chip).
question.explanation: Standard Utah array: 96 electrodes on a 4×4 mm silicon chip, 1.5 mm penetration depth, 100 silicon needles. Multi-electrode arrays in research use 2-4 Utah arrays (192-384 electrodes total). Newer high-density arrays: Neuralink (1024+ per chip), Paradromics (~1600), various university designs (10K+). High electrode count enables more decoding precision + multi-region recording.

question.question: Order these BMI/prosthetic technologies by *level of invasiveness* (least invasive first).
question.explanation:
Invasiveness ranking:
• **EEG cap**: non-invasive, scalp only. Reusable, portable.
• **Surface EMG / myoelectric prosthetic**: non-invasive, on residual limb skin.
• **Stentrode**: minimally invasive (endovascular; deployed via jugular vein into cerebral venous sinus; no craniotomy). Reaches motor cortex; reasonable spatial resolution.
• **ECoG / subdural**: invasive (craniotomy + dural opening); electrode array on cortical surface. Used clinically + research.
• **Utah array**: invasive (craniotomy + insertion); penetrates cortex ~1.5 mm. Records single-unit + LFP. Research + clinical trials.
• **Neuralink threads**: invasive (craniotomy + robotic insertion); penetrates ~3 mm; thinner threads claim less tissue damage but penetrating + deeper than Utah array.

Trade-off: invasive → higher signal quality (10×-100× over EEG) + finer spatial resolution + longer-term degradation issues (encapsulation, scarring). Choice depends on clinical need + research scope + patient + ethical considerations.

question.question: What's the biggest engineering challenge for long-term implantable brain electrodes?
options: Foreign-body response: chronic inflammation + glial scarring (gliosis) encapsulates electrodes within weeks-months, increasing impedance + reducing signal. Penetrating electrodes' performance degrades 30-90% over 1-3 years. Mitigations: soft + flexible electrodes (Neuralink threads, Mesoscale Discovery materials), drug-eluting coatings (dexamethasone), conducting-polymer modifications. Long-term stable cortical recording remains an open challenge.
question.explanation:
**Chronic implantation challenge**: brain tissue treats penetrating electrodes as foreign; engages immune + glial response.

*Foreign-body response (FBR) in CNS*:
1. Acute mechanical injury during insertion: microhemorrhage + BBB disruption.
2. Microglia + astrocytes activate, migrate to electrode within hours.
3. Macrophages + monocytes recruited days-weeks.
4. Astrocytic + microglial encapsulation forms 'glial scar' (200-400 μm thick) within 4-6 weeks.
5. Reduced electrode-neuron contact; impedance rises; signal amplitude drops.

*Specific failure modes*:
- **Single-unit drift**: spiked neurons appear, disappear over weeks. Decoder must adapt.
- **Impedance creep**: increases over time → reduces SNR.
- **Mechanical micro-motion**: brain pulses 0.1-1 mm with heartbeat + respiration; stiff electrodes (silicon, metal) damage tissue + amplify FBR.
- **Material degradation**: corrosion of metals; delamination of insulating coatings.

*Engineering mitigations*:
1. **Soft + compliant electrodes**: polyimide, parylene, hydrogels; Neuralink threads (~5 μm diameter, kgf flexible); MIT-developed mesh electronics. Mechanical mismatch reduced.
2. **Drug-eluting coatings**: dexamethasone (anti-inflammatory) reduces gliosis. ~50-100 day controlled release.
3. **Conducting polymers** (PEDOT, PEDOT-PSS): low impedance + biocompatibility; coating on metal electrodes.
4. **Closed-loop adaptive decoders**: re-calibrate with neural drift; deep-learning approaches.
5. **Glassy carbon + diamond** electrodes: long-term inertness.
6. **Implantation strategy**: insertion speed + technique; some studies suggest slow insertion reduces tissue damage.
7. **Optogenetics + chemogenetics**: optical/genetic alternatives to electrical stimulation; high spatial precision.

*Long-term performance benchmarks*:
- Utah arrays: 5-10 years of usable recordings in some patients; declining signal over years.
- BrainGate cohort longest follow-up: 7+ years.
- Neuralink: only ~6-12 months of human data (as of 2024); long-term unknown.

*Open question*: can we achieve decade-long stable recordings from many channels? Not yet. The 'stable + chronic + high-bandwidth' triangle is the engineering frontier.

This is why BCI is still in clinical trials rather than widely available — long-term reliability + biocompatibility are the bottlenecks.

slides.workedSolution: Foreign-body response: chronic inflammation + glial scarring (gliosis) encapsulates electrodes within weeks-months; signal amplitude declines 30-90% over 1-3 years. Mitigations: soft + flexible electrodes (Neuralink threads, mesh electronics), drug-eluting coatings (dexamethasone), conducting polymers (PEDOT), adaptive decoders. Utah arrays: 5-10 yr usable in some patients. Neuralink: 6-12 mo human data only. Long-term stable high-bandwidth recording is the frontier challenge.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain the ethical considerations for BCI/BMI research + deployment.
question.rubric: Mentions: informed consent — patients with severe disability + limited communication may have impaired consent; need surrogate decision-makers + iterative consent. Risk-benefit: invasive BCI for tetraplegic ALS justifiable; for cognitive enhancement in healthy people much more concerning. Privacy of neural data: emerging concern; Chile + Colorado have neural-rights laws; should brain data be treated like genetic data? Equity + access: $100K-$1M cost; only wealthy + research-eligible patients access. Identity + autonomy: long-term BCI users may experience changes in self-perception. Reversibility: implant removal not always trivial. Industry incentives: rapid commercial development (Neuralink, Synchron, Paradromics) vs academic safety culture. Regulatory pathway: FDA Breakthrough; specialized expertise needed. Open questions: cognitive enhancement boundary; warfare/security; long-term integration with biology. Concludes: BCI ethics emerging field; needs sustained scrutiny + patient-centered governance + public engagement.
